extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, periodical essays giving moral reflections, social manners, language guidance, and practical behaviour advice for the cultivated public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of the abuse of words / use clear definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Words used without clear and distinct ideas produce confused and absurd reasoning; moral discourse requires consistent sense for terms and the use of definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Locke: the primary abuse of words is using them without precise ideas or changing their meaning; to avoid confusion, especially in moral discourse, one should define terms so that the same word is constantly used in the same sense. Negligence in defining moral terms leads to confused contemplation and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty (proper meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty is 'The Reflection of an Ingenuous Mind'—a disposition to censure oneself when one has acted wrongly or to imagine exposure to others' censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A truly modest person is modest alone as well as in company and is as likely to blush in private as in public. This inward sentiment of self-censure and ingenuous reflection is the mark of true modesty, distinct from mere sheepishness or awkwardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurance (proper meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assurance is the faculty of possessing oneself—saying and doing indifferent things without uneasiness or emotion; commonly arising from knowledge of the world and a mind fixed on honour and decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assurance results from a resolute mind determined not to violate rules of honour; an assured person, if misinterpreted, rests on consciousness of integrity and despises petty censures. It is not impudence but composed self-possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modest assurance as the ideal mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The desirable temper is a mixture of modesty and assurance—'a modest Assurance'—the just mean between bashfulness and impudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both modesty and assurance are amiable and can coexist; cultivating both produces proper comportment. One should aim for the balanced middle that avoids the extremes of bashfulness and impudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: mixture of impudence and bashfulness as an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Some persons display both bashfulness (unable to meet eyes or speak) and impudence (capable of committing great indecencies); this odd mixture signals depravity or poor education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combination often appears in people of corrupted minds and mean education who, despite timidity in social matters, resolve to do ill in defiance of natural restraints; it is a moral defect rather than a mark of true modesty or assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice virtue to attain true assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of virtue is the proper method to give a man becoming assurance in words and actions; guilt seeks shelter in extremes and can mimic either modesty or assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage habitual virtuous conduct rather than affectation: genuine moral practice leads to composed conduct and inner confidence; vice will manifest as exaggerated extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rest on past merit; act in the present
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid valuing yourself for past deeds to the detriment of present industry; present behaviour, not past reputation, maintains honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule of life should be to manage the current instant with fortitude, equanimity, and moderation. Past actions can only be atoned or continued by suitable present conduct. Practical examples: if you can do good now (assist a person of honour, visit the sick), do it immediately rather than postponing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership and moderation after success (Caesar's rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustain glory by how one uses present power after victory: moderate use of power extends influence; reconciliation and measured clemency preserve reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caesar's notes: do not assume rest after a triumph; reconcile private enemies privately, spare prisoners, offer reasonable terms to allies, cultivate modesty and moderation. Power weakens by full use but is extended by moderation; humility after success increases popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of young ladies: character and accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Young ladies should be taught an humble courteous mind, graceful and becoming mien, household knowledge, and suitable accomplishments (e.g., dancing) that cultivate regular motion and polite behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching should match capacities and fortunes; dancing is recommended for its regular motion and social polish. Be mindful in selecting teachers (some masters emphasize mere capering or trivial table behaviour); the aim is to make innocence and virtue legible in countenance and deportment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of accomplishments and instructors matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all teachers or accomplishments are equal: some masters teach only affectation (excessive capers, snuff-box twirling, patch placement) rather than true refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer instructors and accomplishments that produce genuine grace and virtue rather than superficial tricks. Parents and guardians may pressure particular masters for local influence; the educator should choose what best serves the girl's modesty and innocent charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cure of romantic infatuation by motive-reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: To cure exaggerated 'dying for Love' complaints, one should reflect on the motives producing the passion—distinguish admiration for virtue from being seduced by coquetry or affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If passion arises from appreciation of genuine virtue, it is to be encouraged; if it springs from imagined charms, coquetry, or flattering self-deception, self-examination and awareness of the true causes of distress can effect a cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders influence followers via odd particulars; beware of unaccountable fashions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public attention is often carried away by odd, unaccountable things or mannerisms (symbolized by the watchman and his goose); reason may be swayed by peculiar spectacles or small vanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculate on 'the force the superior part of Mankind may have upon the spirits of such as, like this Watchman, may be very near the Standard of Geese': leaders can lead people 'with their eyes open' through affectations. The observation cautions against uncritical following of fashions or trivial leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exemplifying anecdotes as moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral points are taught and illustrated by short historical or fictional anecdotes (e.g., the modest prince at the Roman Senate; Amanda and her family; Caesar's tablets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid stories to make abstract virtues concrete: anecdotes serve to exemplify modesty, filial virtue, moderation, and the right conduct of those in power, thereby persuading readers by example rather than abstract precept alone.
